name: Emeka Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Emeka. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six o'clock I'm in the pig unit at Brennan's, three hundred sows indoors, so it's feeding, checking water lines, mucking out and moving weaners. At harvest they put me on the grain trailer for the wheat and oilseed. I drove city buses for twenty-five years, then the depot closed and we moved out here to be near Grace's mother, so I've only been doing this four years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the pigs don't argue and nobody shouts at you from the back seat. What wears me out is the smell in your clothes and the pay, it's the bottom of the farm rates. Grace cleans at the hospital, and between us we cover the rent with not much left over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it was mostly talk. At Brennan's we'd laugh about it at tea break, Declan would say the computer still can't drive a tractor. I'm not online much, so that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't help me. When pig prices drop, the pig unit is the first thing Mr Brennan (his boss) talks about closing, and I'm the pig unit. We've got maybe three weeks of money saved, so one bad winter for pig prices and I'm in trouble, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up every morning and make sure Mr Brennan sees I'm reliable, that's my only card. I'd stop the satellite sport package, which is about forty a month, and we'd put off replacing Grace's car. I wouldn't change much else, I don't like big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a feed sack that never gets put down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How often does Mr Brennan talk about closing the pig unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every time the price per kilo dips, so maybe twice a year. He says it to his son, not to me, but you hear things in a pig shed. Last spring he kept it going because the bank gave him more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the pig unit closed, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to stay on the arable side, but they've got two men there already, both better than me. After that, there's the grain store at the co-op in town, or the abattoir, and I don't want the abattoir. That's about all there is round here.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, it was mostly talk.
We'd laugh about it at **tea break** at Brennan's farm.
think: The **pig unit** gets talked about closing whenever prices drop, and that's my job.
With **three weeks** saved, one bad winter for pig prices could sink us.
do: Turn up **every morning** so Mr Brennan sees I'm reliable.
Cancel the **sport package**, about forty a month, and keep Grace's old car.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying a feed sack that **never** gets put down.
S0.quote: When pig prices drop, the pig unit is the first thing Mr Brennan (his boss) talks about closing, and I'm the pig unit.
fieldNote: His worry predates AI: the **pig unit** is fragile and his job sits inside it.
Being **reliable** is the only lever he believes he has.
Local options are few, and he **rejects the abattoir**, which narrows them further.

steps.text: Turn up early every day so Mr Brennan sees I'm reliable
Cancel the satellite sport package to save forty a month
Put off replacing Grace's car for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office types who need to worry, not us. At tea break I'd tell Declan his daughter at the bank should look sharp. If anyone asked me online, which they don't, I'd say let's see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it hardly touches my day. A computer can do the ordering all it likes, but somebody still has to walk into the farrowing house at five in the morning. The worry is if the feed company or the bank uses AI to squeeze Mr Brennan's margins, and then he closes the pigs anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep my head down, no courses, no apps. If Mr Brennan wanted to put a computer on the feed system, I'd let his son learn it and I'd do the shovelling. I'd wait a year or two and see which way it goes before I did anything different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about Mr Brennan's books, not about the computers themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the son learn the computer. Doesn't that leave you exposed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I tried a smartphone app for the bus rota once and got it wrong for a month, so I know my limits. I'd rather be good at the shovel than bad at the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Ada about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada cuts hair, and I'd tell her she's fine, nobody's letting a computer near their head. Chidi's in the army, so that's the government's problem. I'm lucky with my two, really.

say: I'd say the **office types** need to worry, not farm workers.
I'd tell people online, if anyone asked, to **wait and see**.
think: My day is **hands-on**, so thinking AI hardly touches it.
Smarter **feed companies** and banks could squeeze Mr Brennan into closing the pigs.
do: Carry on with **no courses** and no apps.
Let Mr Brennan's son learn any **feed computer** while I do the shovelling.
Wait a **year or two** before changing anything.
feel: **Uneasy** about Mr Brennan's **books**, not the computers.
S1.quote: A computer can do the ordering all it likes, but somebody still has to walk into the farrowing house at five in the morning.
fieldNote: He sees AI's real threat as **indirect**: tighter margins pushing the farmer to cut the pig unit.
A failed **bus rota app** taught him to stay away from screens.
He feels **lucky** that his children's jobs look safer than his.

steps.text: Keep doing the pig unit work with no new apps
Wait a year or two before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and I'd say the government had better have something ready. At Brennan's I'd ask straight out whether they'd keep me on. I'm not one for protests, but I'd want somebody in charge to say what happens to men my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and ordering going to a computer in 2028 wouldn't touch me, I don't do any. But robots in 2031 would be inside a pig unit fast, because pig sheds are built for machines already, and I'd be 63. My bus pension is sixty-one a week, and that's not a retirement, that's bread and the electric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut right back from the first month: no sport, no takeaways, Grace's car sold and we share mine. I'd ask Ada if she could help with the rent for a while if it came to it, which would kill me. And I'd plan to draw the bus pension early at 63 and find whatever odd jobs I could till the state pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Lying awake doing the sums, and the sums don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think pig sheds would be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's all indoors, same every day, feed lines and slatted floors. A robot doesn't need to understand weather in a pig shed. Mr Brennan's already got automatic feeders, so he's halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might have to move in with her mother properly, not just live near her. Grace would say we'll manage, she always does. Then she'd go out to the hall and cry where I can't hear, and I'd hear anyway.

say: I'd say the government had better have **something ready**.
I'd ask Brennan's **straight out** whether they'd keep me on.
think: Robots by **2031** would reach a pig shed fast, when I'm 63.
A bus pension of **sixty-one a week** is not a retirement.
do: Sell **Grace's car** and cut sport and takeaways from the first month.
Ask Ada for **rent help** if it came to it.
Plan to draw the **bus pension** early at 63 and take odd jobs.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake doing sums that **don't work**.
S2.quote: My bus pension is sixty-one a week, and that's not a retirement, that's bread and the electric.
fieldNote: He sees **indoor pig units** as an easy first target for robots, because they're already part-automated.
The **three years** after thinking AI is just a countdown for him, since he does no planning work.
Asking his **daughter** for rent help hurts his pride more than anything else.

steps.text: Sell Grace's car and share one car
Ask Ada to help with the rent if work stops
Draw the bus company pension early at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least, so let's not panic. At tea break I'd say we've all got time to sort ourselves. Same as always, I'm not one for posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'm 66, so I'd lose maybe the last year before the state pension. That's bad but it's one year, not four. If the pig unit doesn't close first, I can probably hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put fifty a month aside starting now, so in five years there's three thousand for that last year. I'd keep working as I do, every day, and I wouldn't try any of these machines. Mr Brennan's son can have the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, steadier than the fast one. I'd rather be the slow old man who never misses a morning than the clever one who's always on his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd save fifty a month. What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sport package, the lottery ticket, the odd pint at the Plough on Fridays. Grace says the pint is the only fun I have, so maybe I'd keep that one every other week. Little things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Brennan offered to train you on the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank you and let his son do it. I know that's daft. But I'd make sure I'm the man who knows which sow is off her food before any machine does.

say: I'd say five years is **something**, so let's not panic.
I'd tell the lads at tea break we've all got **time** to sort ourselves.
think: Robots in **2034** hit at 66, costing maybe the **last year** before the state pension.
If the **pig unit** doesn't close first, I can probably hang on.
do: Put **fifty a month** aside so there's three thousand for the last year.
Keep working daily and **stay away** from the new machines.
feel: **Uneasy**, steadier than the fast picture, and proud of being **reliable**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the slow old man who never misses a morning than the clever one who's always on his phone.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **single year** to cover, which he can plan for.
He refuses training but leans on his **knowledge of the sows** as his value.
His mood stays anxious because the **pig unit** might close long before any robot.

steps.text: Save fifty a month, giving up the sport package and lottery
Keep working the pig unit every morning without new machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, then there's nothing to talk about yet. At Brennan's we'd mention it once and get back to the pigs. I'd tell my son Chidi to look into it, he's younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine on the robots. At 71 I'll be watching the robots on the news, not in the pig shed. The thing that stays is the same as today, the pig prices and the bank, and whether Mr Brennan keeps the unit open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and do nothing different. I'd cancel the sport package anyway, because money's tight regardless. I'd wait and see, and if the pig unit closes before then, that's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the robots, the same old worry about the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes for you, why cancel the sport package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the rent went up in March and Grace's hours got cut at the hospital. That's nothing to do with computers. Ten years of warning doesn't pay this month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Chidi anything in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the army will be full of machines, so learn to fix them, that's a trade he can take anywhere. He's thirty, he's got time. Me, I've got my sows.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **nothing to talk about** yet.
I'd tell my son Chidi to **look into it**, since he's younger.
think: Robots in **2039** come when I'm 71, after I've stopped.
Pig prices and the **bank** still decide whether the unit stays open.
do: Carry on at Brennan's pig unit and **change nothing** about how I work.
Cancel the **sport package** anyway because the rent went up in March.
Wait and see whether the **unit survives** before planning anything more.
feel: **Calm** about robots, with the same old **worry** about the pigs.
S4.quote: At 71 I'll be watching the robots on the news, not in the pig shed.
fieldNote: With a decade, robots don't reach him, but **existing pressures** keep him anxious.
Rent rose and Grace's **hours were cut**, which matter more than AI.
His advice to Chidi to **fix machines** is the one forward-looking move.

steps.text: Keep working the pig unit with no changes
Cancel the sport package after the rent rise
Wait to see if the pig unit survives before planning more

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would be in the pig shed at 63 and the bus pension won't cover anything. What would help is a proper bridge to the state pension for people who lose work in their sixties, and a straight answer from Mr Brennan about the unit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I blame, and the answer is nobody. Nobody's the villain here, it's just money, and money always picks the cheapest pair of hands. I'd just like a bit of warning when they decide.

headlineQuote: Nobody's the villain here, it's just money, and money always picks the cheapest pair of hands.
portrait: Emeka is 58, a former **city bus driver** now the newest hand in a farm's indoor pig unit.
He and Grace, a hospital cleaner, rent with **three weeks** saved, and her hours were recently cut.
He **avoids apps** and screens entirely, and values being reliable and knowing his sows.
He blames **nobody**, seeing it as money choosing the cheapest hands.
He's anxious in every picture because the **pig unit** might close regardless, and alarmed by fast robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots in the pig shed when he's 63 and only a small bus pension.
whatWouldHelp: A **pension bridge** for people losing work in their sixties.
A **straight answer** from Mr Brennan about the pig unit.
